statement: A strategy is an integrated set of choices that positions an organisation to win, not a document, a target, or an agenda of activities.
implication: Assess a strategy as a set of linked choices. If the parts can be reordered or removed without breaking anything, they were never integrated.
coaching_use: Ask which choice, if reversed, would force every other choice to be redone.

statement: A choice that gives nothing up is not a choice; real strategy closes off options that reasonable people would want to keep open.
implication: The presence of explicit sacrifice is the single fastest signal that a strategy is real.
coaching_use: Ask what the organisation has agreed to be bad at, or to walk away from, as a consequence of this strategy.

statement: Strategy works on the choices inside the organisation's control in order to compel an action by a customer that is not in its control: buying enough, at a price that earns attractive returns, over time.
implication: Both volume and price belong in the success condition. Winning volume at unsustainable prices, or price with too few buyers, is a failed strategy.
coaching_use: Ask what specific customer behaviour would change if this strategy worked, and how they would notice it.

statement: The difference between a plan and a strategy is where the uncertainty sits: plans commit to actions you can execute unilaterally, strategies place bets on how others will respond.
implication: An artefact containing no bet on someone else's behaviour is a plan, however strategic its title.
coaching_use: Ask which part of this could fail even if the organisation executes everything perfectly.

statement: A strategy is a theory about how the organisation will win, and like any theory it can be reasoned about, tested, and disproved - but never proved in advance.
implication: Judge a strategy by the quality of its logic and the honesty of its assumptions, not by the volume of supporting analysis.
coaching_use: Ask what would have to be observed for the team to conclude the theory was wrong.

statement: No amount of analysis produces a provably correct strategy; treating strategy as a data problem trades a hard choice for a comfortable delay.
implication: More analysis is only worth buying when it changes a decision. Otherwise it is cost dressed as rigour.
coaching_use: Ask what decision the next study would change, and what the team would do if it could never be run.

statement: Asking what would have to be true for a possibility to be a great choice separates the logic of the choice from the evidence for it, which lets a group agree on structure before arguing about facts.
implication: Groups that cannot agree on what is true can usually agree on what would need to be true - and that agreement is what makes a decision possible.
coaching_use: Take each option in turn and ask what conditions would have to hold for it to be the obvious answer.

statement: Among the conditions that must be true, the one the team believes least is the barrier to the choice, and it is the only one worth testing first.
implication: Effort spent confirming conditions everybody already believes is wasted; the decision turns entirely on the doubtful condition.
coaching_use: Ask which of the must-be-trues the most sceptical person in the room doubts most.

statement: Test the doubtful condition with the least expensive evidence that would actually change the team's mind.
implication: The design question is not 'what can we learn?' but 'what result would flip this decision?'
coaching_use: Ask what result would settle the question, and what the cheapest way to obtain that result would be.

statement: Strategy work should begin with several genuine possibilities framed as stories of how the organisation could win, not with one recommendation seeking support.
implication: A single option under review invites defence rather than choice; the quality of a decision is bounded by the quality of the alternatives considered.
coaching_use: Ask what the second and third real possibilities were, and why they were set aside.

statement: A strategy cannot rest on what customers, partners or competitors ought to do; it must rest on what they can be expected to do given their own incentives.
implication: Wherever a 'should' appears in the logic, an assumption about someone else's behaviour is being smuggled in unexamined.
coaching_use: Ask why the other party would act that way if they were purely serving their own interest.

statement: Where-to-Play is defined as much by the arenas deliberately left to others as by the ones chosen.
implication: A stated arena that covers everything the organisation currently touches is a description, not a choice.
coaching_use: Ask which customers, geographies or channels this strategy consciously declines to serve.

statement: Some of the most consequential Where-to-Play choices are never discussed because they were inherited - channels, intermediaries, and the stages of the chain the organisation occupies.
implication: Inherited arenas should be surfaced and re-chosen deliberately, or they will quietly constrain the How-to-Win.
coaching_use: Ask which parts of the arena were chosen by this team, and which were simply always there.

statement: Where-to-Play and How-to-Win are a single paired choice; neither can be evaluated without the other.
implication: An arena chosen without a way to win in it is a hope, and a way to win specified without an arena is a slogan.
coaching_use: Ask why this way of winning works better in this arena than in the ones nearby.

statement: Sustainable advantage resolves to being able to serve customers at a lower cost than rivals, or to being different in a way customers will pay for; an organisation that is neither is exposed to whoever is.
implication: A How-to-Win must land on one of these and be honest about the trade-offs the other would have required.
coaching_use: Ask which of the two this strategy is, and what evidence supports the claim relative to named rivals.

statement: Winning is defined against alternatives, not against last year; every claim of advantage is a comparative claim and must name the comparison.
implication: Improvement over one's own past performance is not evidence of advantage.
coaching_use: Ask 'better than whom, at what, in whose judgement?'

statement: A strategy must survive the response of competitors who are also trying to win, including their ability to copy the attractive parts.
implication: If a rival could adopt the same approach without giving anything up, the advantage is temporary at best.
coaching_use: Ask what the strongest competitor would do on hearing this strategy, and what stops them.

statement: Competitive advantage behaves less like a fixed moat and more like a position that has to be re-earned through where the organisation invests its attention and learning.
implication: Strategies premised on a durable structural barrier tend to underinvest in the questions that would keep the advantage alive.
coaching_use: Ask what questions this organisation is working on that its competitors are not yet asking.

statement: The promise made to a customer has to be worth something to them, memorable enough to be recalled at the moment of choice, and specific enough that failure to deliver it would be visible.
implication: Promises that cannot be audited cannot compel action, because nobody - inside or outside - can tell whether they were kept.
coaching_use: Ask how a customer would describe the promise in their own words, and how they would know it had been broken.

statement: Useful customer understanding explains behaviour in context; demographic and size descriptions of a market rarely explain why anyone chooses anything.
implication: Segments that cannot be tied to a difference in behaviour will not support a differentiated How-to-Win.
coaching_use: Ask what these customers do that others do not, and what they are trying to accomplish when they do it.

statement: Capabilities earn their place by being necessary to a specific How-to-Win and by reinforcing each other; a capability that would be equally useful under any strategy is table stakes, not advantage.
implication: A reinforcing system of activities is far harder to copy than any single capability within it.
coaching_use: Ask which capability would become pointless if the How-to-Win changed, and which ones only work because of the others.

statement: Choices survive only if the organisation's systems - what is measured, funded, reviewed and rewarded - are changed to build and protect them.
implication: Unsupported choices decay back to whatever the existing systems already reinforce.
coaching_use: Ask which measure, budget line or standing meeting changes as a direct result of this strategy.

statement: Financial results report on a strategy long after it can be corrected; the measures that matter track the specific behaviours and conditions the strategy's logic depends on.
implication: Every critical assumption should have an indicator attached to it, or the team will learn of failure from the income statement.
coaching_use: Ask which non-financial indicator would move first if the strategy were working, and which if it were failing.

statement: Every choice in a strategy needs a named person with the authority to make it and the boundaries within which it is theirs to make.
implication: Unowned choices are made by default, inconsistently, by whoever is closest to the problem that day.
coaching_use: Ask who owns each choice, and what they are explicitly free to decide without escalation.

statement: Strategy exists at every level and in every function; each level's choices are constrained by the level above and give the level above its capacity to win.
implication: Functions need their own Where-to-Play and How-to-Win expressed in service of the whole, not a translated copy of the corporate deck.
coaching_use: Ask what this strategy asks a specific function or unit to choose differently.

statement: A strategy that cannot be stated plainly by the people who have to act on it cannot guide their daily choices.
implication: Length and polish of the document are unrelated to, and often inversely correlated with, the clarity of the choices.
coaching_use: Ask the team to state the strategy in a few sentences without the deck, then ask who else could do the same.

statement: Strategies fail as often from individually sensible choices that do not add up as from obviously bad ones.
implication: Assessment must test the joints between choices, not just the quality of each choice in isolation.
coaching_use: Walk the cascade in both directions and ask at each step whether the next choice is made easier or harder.

statement: On a landscape with many competing peaks, small adjacent moves give misleading feedback: they can look like progress while leading nowhere worth arriving.
implication: Some strategic questions cannot be answered incrementally, and treating them as such reliably produces local optimisation.
coaching_use: Ask whether this is a step toward a materially different position, or a refinement of the current one.

statement: Organisations get stuck not for lack of options but because the logic behind an old choice has stopped being examined.
implication: Reopening the must-be-trues of the existing strategy is usually more productive than generating new ideas on top of it.
coaching_use: Ask what had to be true when this course was set, and whether those conditions still hold.

statement: A strategy should specify in advance what evidence would justify changing it, so that adaptation is a decision rather than a crisis.
implication: Without pre-agreed disconfirming evidence, teams defend choices past the point where the facts have moved.
coaching_use: Ask what the team would need to see, and by when, to conclude a change of course is required.

statement: Better strategies come from taking the strongest opposing view seriously enough to understand what would make it right, rather than from winning the argument against it.
implication: Disagreement in a strategy discussion is a source of options; suppressing it narrows the choice set to the most senior person's prior.
coaching_use: Ask what the person who disagrees most is seeing that makes their view reasonable.

statement: The aspiration has to be to win at something specific; playing to participate produces choices that avoid loss rather than create advantage.
implication: Aspirations that no competitor could contest are usually descriptions of continued survival.
coaching_use: Ask what winning would look like such that someone else would clearly have lost.

statement: Financial targets are outcomes a strategy might produce, not statements of what winning is or for whom.
implication: A revenue or margin goal gives no guidance about which arena to enter or how to win in it.
coaching_use: Ask what has to be true in the market for that number to appear, and for whom the organisation is winning.
